diagnostic_evidence.quote: Suppose that Assumption \ref{Assumption3-1} and $1.1L(b-a)<1$ hold. Then, for the DE Sinc-collocation method

issues.failure_explanation: The chain (eq:sumeij) replaces the trapezoidal sum h∑_j φ'(jh) by the integral ∫φ'(s)ds = b−a with '≃', and then states (eq:Ebound) and Theorem 3-2 as rigorous inequalities for arbitrary h and N. The trapezoidal sum is not in general ≤ the integral; e.g. for large h (h≈3) the sum is ≈ hφ'(0) = h(b−a)π/4 > 2(b−a), so ‖E‖∞ ≤ 1.1(b−a) is false and the Neumann-series estimate (eq:ImEinvNorm), which needs L‖E‖∞<1, is not justified from 1.1L(b−a)<1 alone. The slack between 1/2+Si(π)/π≈1.092 and 1.1 only covers the trapezoidal error when h is small, which is never assumed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a hypothesis such as h ≤ h0 (satisfied by h = log N/N) and replace '≃' by a standard trapezoidal-rule error estimate for the DE integrand (exponentially small in 1/h) showing h∑φ'(jh) ≤ (b−a)(1+ε) with 1.092(1+ε) ≤ 1.1, or slightly enlarge the constant 1.1.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem 3-2 (and the bound eq:MGSNorm2, its numerical illustration eq:MGSboundsample, and the rough bound on w) is rigorous only under an unstated smallness condition on h; as stated for all h it is false.
issues.title: Bound ‖E‖∞ ≤ 1.1(b−a) in Theorem 3-2 rests on an unquantified trapezoidal approximation and fails for large h
issues.why_classification: A routine local estimate plus a mild, always-satisfied-in-practice condition on h restores the theorem with the same constant and rate; no conclusion is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $p_j(s)$ is a piecewise linear function with $p_j(s_i)=\delta_{ij}$. Then, it is easy to see that $P_j(s_i)=0$ for $i<j$ and the matrix $(w_{ij})$ is lower triangular.

issues.failure_explanation: With φ(s)=s and hat functions p_j, P_j(s_i)=∫_{s_{N_1}}^{s_i} p_j equals h for N_1<j<i, h/2 for j=i (and j=N_1<i), and 0 for j>i. Thus x̃_i = x_a + (h/2)f_{N_1} + h∑_{N_1<j<i} f_j + (h/2) f_i, which is the trapezoidal (Crank–Nicolson) rule, not the implicit Euler method (which would have weights h for all j≤i, j>N_1). The prose asserts an identification that the construction does not support.

failure_location.quote: In fact, this method is nothing but the implicit Euler method and the lower triangularity means that the method respects causality

issues.overall_effect: Only the heuristic identification in Subsection 3.3 is wrong; the lower-triangularity/causality point and all theorems are unaffected.
issues.title: Identity transformation with piecewise-linear interpolation is misidentified as the implicit Euler method
issues.why_classification: A one-word correction with no effect on any result or argument.

issues.failure_explanation: For Example 3 on [0,1] with ρ=1/2, the bound M on ‖f‖∞ over D'_ρ is at least 5/2 (x_1=5/2, x_2=1), so ρ/M ≤ 1/5 while w ≈ b−a = 1, violating Assumption 3-1(iii); and the Lipschitz constant satisfies L ≥ 2.5 (Jacobian row (x_2, x_1, 0) at the initial point), so 1.1L(b−a) ≥ 2.75 > 1, violating the hypothesis of Theorem 3-2 and making the bound (eq:MGSNorm2) meaningless (negative denominator). The paper nevertheless includes Example 3, with a figure of 'its upper bound', among examples claimed to confirm Theorems 3-1 and 3-2, without verifying (and without any possibility of satisfying) the hypotheses.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either shrink the interval of Example 3 (and choose ρ, M, L) so that Assumption 3-1(iii) and 1.1L(b−a)<1 verifiably hold, or state explicitly that Example 3 lies outside the theory and drop the 'upper bound' curve.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For general $m$ and $A(0)$, the matrix exponential $\exp(tA(0))$ has to be calculated numerically.

issues.failure_explanation: For a tridiagonal A(0) with m ≥ 3, exp(tA(0)) is a full matrix and its LR (LU) factors are in general full unit lower triangular and full upper triangular; no factorization with bidiagonal R_t (or bidiagonal L_t) exists. Only the conjugated matrix A(t)=L_t^{-1}A(0)L_t is tridiagonal. The description of step (ii) therefore demands a factorization that does not exist for general m (it coincides with the ordinary LR decomposition only for m=2, the case actually used).

failure_location.quote: Compute $\exp(tA(0))$ and its $LR$ decomposition $\exp(tA(0))=L_t R_t$, where $L_t$ is a unit lower subdiagonal matrix and $R_t$ is an upper bidiagonal matrix.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the shape descriptors by 'L_t unit lower triangular and R_t upper triangular' (the standard LR decomposition).
issues.overall_effect: The general-m procedure in Appendix B is misdescribed; the m=2 example and the Lotka–Volterra exact solution (eq:LV3sol1–3) are unaffected.
issues.title: LR factors of exp(tA(0)) are wrongly described as unit lower bidiagonal / upper bidiagonal for general m
issues.why_classification: A one-phrase correction; the procedure and all results using it survive unchanged.
